title: LIGO: Catching the Whisper of Colliding Black Holes
source_book: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters 116)
source_author: B. P. Abbott et al. (LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration)
authenticity_note: Directly derived from the historic September 14, 2015 detection of event GW150914 by the two LIGO laser interferometers in Hanford, WA, and Livingston, LA, exactly 100 years after Einstein's prediction.
summary: A billion light-years away, two gargantuan black holes spiraled into each other at half the speed of light and merged. On September 14, 2015, the twin LIGO laser interferometers caught the resulting ripple in spacetime—measuring a distortion ten-thousand times smaller than a single proton and opening a completely new sensory window on the cosmos.
content:
In 1916, Albert Einstein published his General Theory of Relativity, predicting that the violent acceleration of colossal cosmic masses—such as colliding dead suns—would produce ripples in the fabric of spacetime, spreading across the cosmos at the speed of light like waves on a pond. Yet Einstein was convinced humans would never detect them: by the time these waves reached Earth from deep space, their distortion would be smaller than the nucleus of an atom!

For forty years, physicists Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, and Barry Barish championed an audacious dream: build an observatory to catch Einstein's ripples using laser interferometry.

They constructed the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO)—two identical L-shaped observatories separated by 3,000 kilometers, one in Livingston, Louisiana, and the other in Hanford, Washington. Each arm stretched 4 kilometers through giant vacuum tubes. A laser beam was split in two, bounced back and forth between mirrors hanging on glass fibers, and recombined. If a gravitational wave passed through Earth, it would stretch one 4-kilometer arm by a fraction of a hair while squeezing the other, shifting the recombined light waves.

How sensitive was LIGO? It could measure a change in length equivalent to one ten-thousandth the diameter of a single subatomic proton across four kilometers!

On September 14, 2015, at 09:50:45 UTC, just days after an advanced upgrade, a signal swept through Earth.

First, the Livingston detector recorded an unmistakable, rising oscillating wave. Exactly 7 milliseconds later—the precise time required for light to travel across the continent—the exact same signal struck Hanford!

The signal was designated **GW150914**. Analysis revealed that 1.3 billion years ago, two black holes—one 29 times the mass of our Sun, the other 36 times—had whirled around each other 250 times per second at half the speed of light, before smashing together. In a fraction of a second, three solar masses of pure matter were converted into pure gravitational energy, releasing more power than all the stars in the observable universe combined!

When the frequency was converted into sound, scientists heard a rising 'chirp'—the heartbeat of two black holes kissing in the dark. Humanity was no longer merely watching the universe through light; for the first time, we had learned to hear the music of spacetime itself.

The stretching and squeezing of physical space and time predicted by Einstein's General Relativity.
